Nadab
NAY-dab
proper noun (figure)
Hebrew Nadab (H5070) — "generous, willing, noble," from the root nadab ("to incite, offer voluntarily"). The same name was borne by Aaron's eldest son (Lev 10:1-2, killed for strange fire) and by this second king of Israel.

📖 Biblical Definition

Nadab (c. 910 — 909 BC) was the second king of the divided northern kingdom of Israel (1 Kings 15:25-31), son of Jeroboam I son of Nebat. His two-year reign was the entire duration of the Jeroboam dynasty after its founder. He continued in his father's golden-calf apostasy at Bethel and Dan, and was assassinated while besieging the Philistine city of Gibbethon by his military commander Baasha, who then proceeded to kill every male of Jeroboam's house in fulfillment of Ahijah the Shilonite's earlier prophecy (1 Kings 14:10-11). His brief reign is the first instance of the recurring divided-monarchy pattern: a king continues in Jeroboam's sin; the LORD's prophet-pronounced judgment falls; the dynasty is extinguished; the assassin becomes king and continues the same apostasy.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Second king of Israel (c. 910-909 BC); son of Jeroboam I; reigned 2 years; assassinated by Baasha at the siege of Gibbethon; all males of Jeroboam's house then killed in fulfillment of Ahijah's prophecy.

NADAB, proper noun. Hebrew Nadab (H5070) — "generous, willing, noble."

Second king of the divided northern kingdom of Israel (c. 910-909 BC); son of Jeroboam I.

Two-year reign; continued the golden-calf apostasy; assassinated by Baasha at the siege of Gibbethon (1 Kings 15:27-28).

Distinct from Nadab the son of Aaron (Lev 10:1-2), killed for strange fire.

📖 Key Scripture

1 Kings 15:25-26 — "And Nadab the son of Jeroboam began to reign over Israel in the second year of Asa king of Judah, and reigned over Israel two years. And he did evil in the sight of the LORD, and walked in the way of his father, and in his sin wherewith he made Israel to sin."

1 Kings 15:27-28 — "And Baasha the son of Ahijah, of the house of Issachar, conspired against him; and Baasha smote him at Gibbethon, which belonged to the Philistines... Even in the third year of Asa king of Judah did Baasha slay him, and reigned in his stead."

1 Kings 14:10 — "Therefore, behold, I will bring evil upon the house of Jeroboam, and will cut off from Jeroboam him that pisseth against the wall."

Leviticus 10:1-2 — "And Nadab and Abihu, the sons of Aaron... offered strange fire before the LORD, which he commanded them not. And there went out fire from the LORD, and devoured them."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Nadab is corrupted when his short reign is treated as merely a transitional curiosity rather than as the first instance of the recurring divided-monarchy coup-and-judgment pattern, or when his name is conflated with Aaron's son Nadab who died for strange fire.

expand to see more

Two different Nadabs. The name Nadab appears in Scripture for at least two important figures: Aaron's eldest son (Lev 10:1-2), who together with his brother Abihu was struck dead for offering strange fire in the wilderness tabernacle, and this second king of Israel (1 Kings 15:25). Popular Sunday-school treatment sometimes conflates them or treats Nadab-the-king as a footnote. They are entirely distinct figures separated by roughly five centuries; both share the irony that their name means 'willing/generous' yet both ended in divine judgment.

Transitional-king dismissal. Nadab's two-year reign is sometimes skipped in surveys of the divided monarchy. The Chronicler-style narrator in 1 Kings 15 highlights it precisely because it inaugurated the recurring pattern: a dynasty established by Jeroboam's choice to lead Israel into the golden-calf cult could not last more than one generation because the prophetic judgment had already been pronounced. The lesson is doctrinal-generational: covenant rejection produces dynastic destruction, however brief the second-generation reign.
